title: Intrinsic notes in the matter itself: history, prophecy, and dogma; sacred history's claim to truth
pass_a_gloss: Turning next to Scripture's own subject-matter: marks of divinity still more illustrious and clearer show themselves there. Everything contained in Scripture falls into histories and narrations of past events, or oracles and predictions of future events, or dogmas and precepts that mark no difference of time. A history is chiefly recommended by two things: the truth of what is told, and also its weight and moment — and sacred history claims both in an eminent degree. First, sacred history has many great indications of truth. Either reason and the very nature of things give it suffrage — as with the history of the world's creation, proved by the strongest arguments to have been made from nothing and in time — or, for history, monuments of ancient and external writers also witness to its truth: for example the universal flood, the building of Babel's tower, the burning of Sodom and Gomorrah, and Israel's exit from Egypt, mentioned among approved ancient historians whose fragments survive in Eusebius, Josephus, and others, some of them still current in men's hands.
pass_b_english: Now if we attend to the things themselves of Scripture, notes of divinity still far more illustrious and clearer will appear in them. Whatever Scripture contains is either histories and narrations of things past, or oracles and predictions of things future, or dogmas and precepts that mark no difference of time. Further, two things chiefly commend a history: the truth of the matters, and also their weight and moment — both of which sacred history claims for itself in an eminent way. And first, sacred history has many and great indications of truth. For either reason and the very nature of things give it suffrage, as with the history of the world's creation, which is proved by most strong arguments to have been made from nothing and in time. As for history, even the monuments of ancient and external writers also afford testimony to its truth — for example in the history of the universal flood, of the building of the tower of Babel, of the burning of Sodom and Gomorrah, of the Israelites' exit from Egypt — of which mention is made among approved and ancient historians whose fragments survive in Eusebius, Josephus, and others, and some of which are still current in men's hands.
source_text: XXXVIII. Jam vero, si ad res ipsas Scripturae attendamus, in iis apparebunt longe adhuc illustriores et clariores divinitatis notae. Quaecunque autem Scriptura continentur vel sunt historiae et narrationes rerum praeteritarum, vel sunt vaticinia et praedictiones rerum futurarum, vel dogmata et praecepta quae nullam temporis differentiam notant. Porro historiam praecipue duo commendant, nempe rerum veritas, tum quoque pondus et momentum: quae duo Historia sacra eminenti quodam modo sibi vendicat. Et primo quidem historia sacra multa et magna habet veritatis indicia. Vel enim illi ratio, et ipsa rerum natura suffragatur, ut historiae creationis mundi, quem e nihilo atque in tempore factum esse validissimis probatur argumentis. Ut historiae, eorum etiam veterum et externorum monumenta testimonium ejus veritati perhibent, ut ex. gr. in historia de diluvio universali, de aedificatione turris Babylonicae, de conflagratione Sodomae et Gomorrhae, de Israelitarum exitu ex Aegypto, quibus mentio fit apud probatos et priscos historicos quorum fragmenta supersunt apud Eusebium, Josephum et alios: et nonnulli etiam in manibus hominum versantur.
